title: What Our Irrigation AI Gets Wrong (And Why We're Keeping It Anyway)
subtitle: 18 months of inference-based irrigation scheduling: the wins, the failures, and the cases where the model confidently does the wrong thing
author: priya-nandakumar
body_text:
I keep a paper notebook. It sits next to my laptop in the office space and it contains, in my own handwriting, a log of every time the Drip inference engine issued a prediction that turned out to be wrong in a way I think is worth understanding. The notebook has 47 entries over 18 months.

This is not a story about a model that works perfectly. It's a story about a model that works well enough to be useful while failing in specific ways that are worth documenting publicly, because I think most ML deployments in real physical systems fail similarly and talk about it rarely.

Drip — our irrigation inference engine — runs on an XGBoost regression model, one per farm zone. Each model takes 42 input features: soil moisture readings from all Rhizome nodes in the zone, temperature at depth, historical weather, current weather, crop type and phenological stage, days since last irrigation, and several derived features like rate-of-change of VWC. It outputs a recommended irrigation duration for the next 4-hour window. A separate scheduling layer converts that into actual valve open times.

We've been running it in production for 18 months. In aggregate, it works. Water use is down roughly 31% compared to our previous time-based schedule, with no statistically significant yield change across three production seasons. I'm proud of those numbers.

But the notebook.

**The First Frost Problem**

The model handles gradual seasonal transitions reasonably well — it's seen three full growing cycles now and has enough temperature and phenological data to calibrate for summer-to-fall transitions. What it does not handle well is sudden discontinuities.

Our first hard frost event last November came 11 days earlier than any frost in our 4-year weather dataset. The model, asked to predict irrigation needs for the day after that frost, extrapolated from its training distribution and issued near-normal irrigation recommendations for crops that were about to die or go dormant. It had never seen a frost that early in the season in context with those specific crop-stage feature values. It had no basis for the right answer.

We caught this because we still have a morning briefing where someone reviews the day's scheduled irrigation before valves open. Felix looked at the frost forecast and the irrigation schedule side by side and flagged it. We overrode manually.

This is in my notebook as an annotation about the limits of interpolation. The model is really an interpolation engine over its training data. When you push it to genuinely novel conditions, it interpolates from the nearest training examples, which may be quite wrong. We now have an explicit frost-check pre-processor that flags any predicted frost within 72 hours and holds the model's recommendations for human review.

**The Confident Wrong Answer Problem**

Gradient boosted trees don't give you uncertainty estimates natively. The model outputs a number: irrigate zone 3 for 18 minutes. It does not say: I'm 60% confident in this, or: I've only seen this feature combination 12 times in training. It just gives you the number.

This becomes a problem in proportion to how much you trust the number. We went through a phase, around month 8, where we had stopped manually reviewing recommendations as carefully because it had been working reliably for months. We lost a sense of the model's confidence calibration.

The wake-up call was a peculiar week in February where we had unusually warm days followed by cold nights, with low humidity and high winds. The model issued low irrigation recommendations based on cool temperatures, when in fact VPD (vapor pressure deficit) was extremely high due to the dry wind, and the crops were water-stressed despite the cool temperatures.

The fix was partly technical — we added VPD as an explicit feature, which the model had been computing indirectly but not well — and partly procedural. We reinstated a daily human review of the scheduled irrigation against a basic sanity check: current weather conditions, visible plant appearance, and gut feel from whoever's been in the field that morning.

Gut feel sounds like capitulation to vagueness. It isn't. An experienced grower looking at plants can detect water stress that no sensor we have is measuring. We should always want that in the loop.

**What The Model Gets Consistently Right**

Since I've been cataloguing failures, I should be fair about the wins.

The model is excellent at distinguishing between days that look similar by calendar and temperature but differ in crop water demand due to growth stage. It learned to track phenological indicators — bloom timing, fruit set, senescence — that we'd never thought to formalize in our manual scheduling. Before the model, we adjusted irrigation by season and rough crop stage. The model adjusts by something finer than that, and it's mostly right.

It's also good at the boring optimization — knowing that zone 7 can go an extra four hours without irrigation because its clay content buffers moisture differently than zone 3's sandier profile. It holds this calibration across the whole growing season without forgetting, which humans do.

**Should You Build Something Like This?**

Only if you have the sensor density to support it. Without the Rhizome network as input, the Drip model would be roughly useless. The model is only as good as the feature data it receives, and coarse sensor coverage would give it coarse input to reason from.

Also: keep the human in the loop, visibly and consequentially. Not as a rubber stamp, but as a genuine review step with the authority and expectation of overriding the model when warranted. A model that's overridden 5% of the time is being used correctly. A model that's never overridden has become an authority it shouldn't be.

title: Automating Greenhouse Climate: Everything Works Except Humidity
subtitle: Temperature, CO2, and lighting are solved problems for us. Humidity has humbled us repeatedly.
author: yuki-tanigawa
body_text:
I want to be careful about how I frame this, because I don't want to sound dismissive of what the Canopy system does well. Temperature control in Greenhouse A is genuinely solved — we maintain setpoint within ±0.5°C continuously, across a 35°C swing in outdoor conditions, with good energy efficiency. CO2 supplementation runs on a timed schedule with sensor validation that keeps us at target within ±50ppm. Supplemental lighting follows a sophisticated photoperiod model that Priya and I built together over two growing seasons. These things work.

Humidity does not work. Or rather, it works in the easy cases and fails in ways that are expensive and frustrating in the hard ones.

Let me explain why humidity is harder than it looks.

**Why Humidity Control Is Harder Than Temperature**

Temperature is a single variable with straightforward physics. You heat or cool, and the system responds predictably. You can build a PID controller for temperature in an afternoon and have it working well within a week of tuning.

Humidity is not a single variable. Relative humidity (RH) is a function of both actual moisture content in the air and temperature. When the temperature changes, the RH changes, even if no moisture has entered or left the system. This coupling means your humidity control loop and your temperature control loop interact in ways that require careful coordination.

Beyond the physics, greenhouses have moisture sources that temperature-controlled rooms do not: transpiring plants. A mature cucumber canopy in high-production summer conditions moves a remarkable amount of water vapor. This is a distributed, variable, biologically-driven moisture source that changes with plant growth stage, light levels, temperature, and health. You cannot measure it directly. You can only manage its effects.

**What The Current System Does**

Canopy v3 runs separate PID control loops for temperature and humidity, with a coordination layer that resolves conflicts (you can't simultaneously heat and dehumidify efficiently, for example). Humidity control uses a combination of roof vent actuation, circulation fans, and — when needed — an electric dehumidifier as a high-cost last resort.

The architecture is sound. The tuning is where we've spent most of our effort.

The main failure mode is what I've started calling transition instability — the period between day and night setpoints (or any other transition event) where the system oscillates before settling. At night, we drop the temperature setpoint by 6–8°C, which causes a corresponding RH increase. The system responds by trying to reduce humidity, which requires ventilation, which also drops temperature faster than intended, which triggers heating, which changes humidity dynamics, and so on. In a well-designed, well-insulated climate chamber, these dynamics are predictable enough to tune for. In a working greenhouse with plants, uneven air distribution, and a permeable structure, they're harder.

We've had nights where the humidity oscillation during the day-to-night transition caused RH to spike above 90% for 15–20 minutes before the system corrected. That's not catastrophic, but it's a recurring Botrytis risk on susceptible crops.

**Three Things We've Tried**

Model predictive control (MPC) instead of pure PID: We implemented an MPC approach that uses weather forecast data to pre-condition the greenhouse before transitions — starting to adjust humidity before the temperature setpoint change rather than reacting to it. This helped significantly. Transition instability is now about half as severe as it was. We haven't fully replaced the PID approach, though — the MPC is used only for predictable transitions and the PID handles unexpected events.

Spatial averaging with zone weighting: We found that our single-point humidity sensors were inadequate for representing a greenhouse with significant air stratification. We added 8 humidity sensors per greenhouse at different heights and positions, and the control loop now operates on a weighted average that accounts for the sensor positions relative to the crops. This caught some systematic errors we'd been living with.

Plant growth stage compensation: Yuki-specific addition to Canopy v3. Because I track plant phenology for the cultivar trials, I wrote a small adjustment module that modifies the humidity setpoints slightly based on growth stage. Young transplants and mature fruiting plants want different VPD regimes. Having these as explicit inputs to the control system rather than implicit assumptions has helped, mostly in the seedling stage where our previous system was keeping conditions too dry.

**What I Don't Know Yet**

Whether our current approach to nighttime humidity management is actually optimal, or whether we've just found a local optimum we've become comfortable with. The literature suggests that dynamic night humidity targets (higher early night, lower late night) might perform better than our current fixed target, but I haven't built that experiment yet.

Whether the residual humidity spikes we still get are causing measurable plant health impacts. We have some correlational evidence that our Botrytis incidence is lower in years with better humidity control, but we can't isolate it from other variables cleanly.

The honest summary: the automation makes our greenhouse climate more consistent and less labor-intensive than manual management. It also exposes clearly how complex greenhouse climate actually is — things we previously attributed to 'the vagaries of the weather' are now attributable to specific control failures we can work on. I find that progress, even though it means the to-do list never gets shorter.

title: The Mobile Coop Robot: Speed Was the Only Thing That Mattered
subtitle: We built a robot to move a chicken coop. We got the engineering right on the first try and the animal behavior wrong on the first three.
author: tobias-kellenbrink
body_text:
Wanderer — our mobile coop platform — is the most mechanically boring robot on the property. Four-wheel drive electric vehicle, buried wire guidance system, simple PLC control logic, load cell on the hitch for safety cutoff. There is nothing interesting about it from an engineering standpoint. I say this without embarrassment. The interesting part was entirely about chicken behavior, and we had to get burned three times before we understood it.

**The Problem We Were Solving**

We run a rotational grazing system with our poultry flock. The coop moves along a defined grid across the pasture, allowing each section to recover before the birds return. When we were doing this manually, the move happened twice a week — someone would hitch a tractor to the coop, drive 6 meters, unhitch, and go do something else. Twenty-minute task, twice a week. Not burdensome.

But 'not burdensome' and 'actually done consistently' are different things on a farm with 40 people, variable schedules, and a long task list. The coop moves were getting skipped, delayed, or done at irregular intervals that compromised the rotation timing. The pasture recovery data showed it.

The automation brief was to move the coop daily, 4–6 meters, without requiring any human decision-making or physical labor. Get the timing consistent.

**The First Version: It Worked. The Chickens Hated It.**

Prototype v1 moved at what I considered a reasonable working speed: 1.5 meters per second. The coop covers 6 meters in about four seconds at that speed. Quick, efficient, done.

The chickens were in the coop during the first test. We always move the coop with the birds inside — this is standard practice in rotational systems, moving them to fresh pasture rather than opening the door and hoping they follow.

At 1.5m/s, the interior of the coop lurches forward. Water nipples slosh. Feed spills. The perches vibrate. The birds went into complete alarm behavior. They piled into the corners, which in a full coop of 180 birds creates dangerous crowding. We stopped immediately.

Okay, we thought. Slower.

v1.1 moved at 0.8m/s. Better, but still significant distress. Clustering behavior, alarm vocalizations, reduced laying rates for two days following each move. Felix was clear that this was unacceptable as a routine practice.

v1.2 moved at 0.4m/s. The birds tolerated it. No alarm clustering. Laying rates unaffected. We thought we had it.

**The Second Problem: The Birds Wanted to Walk**

We had been thinking about the coop move as a transportation event — move the structure, birds inside, to the new location. This is how it works with a tractor: the move is fast, the birds are in the coop, they can't do anything about it.

At 0.4m/s on a daily move, the birds can absolutely do something about it. They can walk alongside the coop and enter through the pop holes rather than riding inside it.

Within a week of deploying v1.2, a significant portion of the flock had figured this out. The coop would start moving, the birds inside would feel the motion, pop out through the doors, and join the ones who were already walking alongside. This was, behaviorally, much calmer and apparently preferred by the birds.

But it created a management problem: we needed all the birds inside the coop at night when the move finished, and we had no way to ensure that. Some birds were following the coop all the way to the new location. Others were drifting. By the time the coop stopped at its new position, we had a distributed flock that needed mustering.

Not what we wanted to automate.

**The Third Problem: They Associated the Sound with Movement**

Before we'd figured out the walking-alongside problem, we hit another one. The Wanderer motor system makes a distinctive low hum when engaged. The birds learned this within two weeks. Before the coop had moved a centimeter, any bird near the coop would register the motor sound and begin exiting or showing pre-alarm behavior.

This is actually not a bad thing from a welfare standpoint — predictable cues give animals agency, which reduces stress. But it meant that the flock was moving before the coop was moving, which complicated our fence management (we use temporary poultry net that needs to be repositioned ahead of the move).

**The Design That Actually Works**

Current Wanderer, v2.1, works as follows: it moves at 0.28m/s maximum. The motor sound cue happens naturally and consistently (we stopped trying to muffle it — it's a useful signal for the birds). Fence repositioning happens 20 minutes before the scheduled move time, which we learned is about when the birds start anticipating based on morning light levels plus the fence crew's presence. When the coop starts moving, we open all pop holes — both the usual exit doors and two additional low-side hatches we added specifically for walk-alongside birds. The floor of the coop has been modified so that the motion at 0.28m/s creates minimal internal disturbance.

Result: about 60% of the flock rides the coop; 40% walks alongside. Both groups arrive at the new location within a few minutes of each other. The pop holes close on a timer after full arrival, confirmed by a simple count from a camera we installed over the coop entrance.

The automation is real. The move now happens daily, at consistent times, with no human involvement beyond occasionally checking the camera count. Felix reports that flock health metrics — laying rates, behavior indicators, weight gain in the broilers — are the best they've been since we started the rotational system.

But the design came from watching the birds, not from engineering. Every substantive change we made was driven by observing what the chickens actually did with the system we'd built, and adjusting. This is, I suppose, the recurring theme from this year: build for the biology first, build the robot second.
